title: The One With The Vows

jokes.text: Four weeks, baby. Four weeks! / Do you realize you get louder each week?
jokes.setup: Chandler enthusiastically echoes Monica's countdown about their approaching wedding.
jokes.punchline: Monica dryly notes that his volume increases with each passing week of excitement.
jokes.explanation: Solid opener establishing the wedding-stress dynamic. Monica's deadpan observation is a clean, competent joke. Fits both characters well but isn't particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're getting married!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, we are.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: WE'RE GETTING MARRIED!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And apparently the further away the wedding is, the louder you have to yell about it.

jokes.text: I figured I'd just buy those. 'Pat, I'd like to buy a vow.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks if Chandler has written his wedding vows.
jokes.punchline: Chandler jokes he'd just buy them, riffing on 'Wheel of Fortune' ('I'd like to buy a vowel').
jokes.explanation: A clever wordplay joke ('vowel'/'vow') that also perfectly captures Chandler's deflection-through-humor personality. The Wheel of Fortune reference is well-deployed and economical. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Have you written your vows yet?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'd like to buy a vowel.

jokes.text: You know I've no sense of humor when it comes to the wedding.
jokes.setup: Chandler makes the vow-buying joke.
jokes.punchline: Monica's humorless, overly serious response IS the joke — the audience knows Monica well enough that this is exactly on-brand.
jokes.explanation: Works almost entirely on character integration — Monica's wedding obsession is a well-established running gag and this line lands because the audience knows exactly who she is. The joke is Monica herself being the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I have no sense of humor about my wedding.

jokes.text: With Carol, I promised never to love another woman until the day I die. She made no such promise.
jokes.setup: Monica asks Ross what he said in his previous wedding vows to help her write hers.
jokes.punchline: Ross reveals his vow was completely one-sided — and Carol didn't reciprocate, which is darkly funny given she left him for a woman.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The two-sentence structure is devastatingly economic — the first sentence sounds sincere and romantic, the second sentence is an atomic bomb delivered with casual understatement. Layers of meaning: Carol's infidelity, Ross's obliviousness, and the cruelty of the original vow now being comically absurd. High quotability, excellent character integration (only Ross's backstory makes this work).

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm writing my vows and I can't stop! I've already filled three pages!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Three pages? Monica, vows aren't a hostage negotiation. How long are you planning to make yours?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know, as long as it takes to express how I feel.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I'm on page four. So I win.

jokes.text: I like the pretty drawing of you in the wedding dress. Except your breasts look kind of small.
jokes.setup: Monica shows Joey her vow-writing attempt, which apparently contains a sketch.
jokes.punchline: Joey critiques the drawing for having small breasts.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey — his brain goes immediately to breasts when looking at any drawing of a woman. The setup (showing vows) and punchline (breast critique) works because it's so perfectly in character. Not high craft but reliable Joey comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What's wrong with me?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, no. Don't go there.

jokes.text: Those are my eyes! / Those are my breasts.
jokes.setup: Joey says the drawn breasts look small; Monica corrects that he's looking at her eyes.
jokes.punchline: Monica then clarifies where her actual drawn breasts are, inadvertently confirming Joey's interest.
jokes.explanation: A quick escalation of the previous joke — the punchline is Monica pointing out her actual drawn breasts, which continues the absurdity. Tight two-beat structure with good audience satisfaction.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, there are no words...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, actually, there are words. A lot of words. But none of them are appropriate.

jokes.text: Monica, from the moment I met you, I knew I loved you. [flashback] Everyone, this is Chandler. Hi, I'm Ross' little sister.
jokes.setup: Phoebe suggests Chandler open his vows with 'from the moment I met you, I knew I loved you.'
jokes.punchline: Flashback reveals their actual first meeting — Chandler is completely indifferent and Monica introduces herself as Ross's little sister, suggesting zero romantic spark.
jokes.explanation: Effective misdirection — a romantic suggestion immediately undercut by the mundane reality of their history. The 'Hi, I'm Ross's little sister' line is funny because it's so utterly unromantic. Works as a structural device for the episode's flashback format.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What did you say in your vows?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I promised to love her forever, to be faithful, to support her dreams...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And what did Carol say?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She said 'I do' and then six months later 'I'm leaving you for a woman.'

jokes.text: All right, there's a nuclear holocaust. I'm the last man on earth. Would you go out with me?
jokes.setup: Monica's flashback shows her being immediately uninterested in Chandler at their first meeting; Phoebe suggests he say he always wanted more from their friendship.
jokes.punchline: Chandler sarcastically demonstrates how preposterous that claim is by proposing only the most extreme hypothetical scenario where Monica would date him.
jokes.explanation: Chandler self-deprecation at its best. The nuclear holocaust escalation is absurdist but grounded — it reflects how out-of-his-league he felt Monica was. High character integration and quotability. The word 'holocaust' is a surprising dark choice that makes the joke land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Is that the dress? Because it looks like you drew a uterus.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That is not a uterus!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, okay. Well, then where's the neck?

jokes.text: Are we allowed to lie in the vows?
jokes.setup: Monica's reaction to the nuclear holocaust joke implies the flashback memory is not flattering.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's deadpan follow-up: asking if lying is permitted in wedding vows.
jokes.explanation: A punchy follow-up to the previous bit. 'Are we allowed to lie in the vows?' is a crisp, economical joke that maximizes Chandler's self-deprecating persona. Good economy of words.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, this is my friend Chandler. Chandler, this is my sister Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hi Monica. So, uh, do you believe in love at first sight, or should I walk by again?

jokes.text: The erogenous zones flashback — Monica teaching Chandler the seven erogenous zones on a drawing, culminating in the famous 'Seven!' sequence
jokes.setup: Phoebe suggests Chandler's vows mention things Monica taught him; this triggers the flashback of Monica's erogenous zones lesson
jokes.punchline: The sequence escalates to Monica repeating 'seven' with increasing intensity — a callback to one of the show's most beloved running gags, landing as pure joy for the audience
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's highest-impact moment by audience reaction. The 'seven' bit is one of Friends' most iconic recurring gags, and its deployment here as a flashback in a vows-writing context is structurally brilliant — it's both nostalgic fan service AND an earned character beat (Monica teaching Chandler intimacy is literally what made him fall for her). The escalating numeric sequence into the climactic 'SEVEN!' is perfectly constructed comedy. Impact is a 9 because a room of Friends fans would erupt. Craft slightly lower because it's largely borrowed capital from the original scene.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So there are all these erogenous zones on a woman's body.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. You're telling me there are erogenous zones I don't know about?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes! Like the small of the back, behind the ears, the inside of the wrist...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The inside of the wrist? What am I supposed to do, lick it like a stamp?

jokes.text: That's one? / Kind of an important one.
jokes.setup: Monica is pointing out erogenous zones on a diagram or body; apparently zone #1 is not where Chandler expected.
jokes.punchline: Monica confirms it is indeed zone one — 'kind of an important one' — delivered with matter-of-fact authority.
jokes.explanation: Monica's authoritative understatement 'kind of an important one' is very on-brand and gets laughs. Part of the sustained erogenous zone sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, there's your problem.

jokes.text: I was looking at it upside down. / Well, you know, sometimes that helps.
jokes.setup: Chandler is confused about which body part is zone #1 because he was looking at the diagram upside down.
jokes.punchline: Monica confirms that sometimes looking at the erogenous zone upside down does help — delivered completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The delivery of this joke is key — Monica's straight-faced confirmation that upside down viewing sometimes helps is a great deadpan moment. Keeps the erogenous zone sequence building.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so you start here, very lightly...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Then you move to here, a little bit harder...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And then you can really go to town right... here.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Seven! Seven! Seven!

jokes.text: Okay, now, start out with a little one... a two, a one-two-three... a three, a five... a four, a three-two... two, a two-four-six. Two-four-six, four, two... two, four-seven... five-seven, six-seven... seven, seven... seven, seven, seven, seven, seven... seven!
jokes.setup: Monica has been teaching Chandler the seven erogenous zones; now she demonstrates the sequence, apparently physically touching him as she calls out numbers.
jokes.punchline: The escalating '7, 7, 7!' chant as Monica reaches the climax of the instructional sequence, clearly implying a sexual crescendo through numbered zones.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout moment of the episode and one of the most iconic Friends gags. The escalating numbers function as a coded sexual crescendo that is simultaneously hilarious and completely plausible as an earnest sex-ed tutorial from Monica. The structure is flawless — it builds, it escalates, and the climactic 'SEVEN!' is a perfect payoff. High quotability, perfect character integration (only Monica could deliver this with such enthusiastic, clinical authority), and genuine originality in its execution. The extended repetition of 'seven' is exactly as long as it needs to be.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, twins! Look at them, they're so perfect. One for me, one for Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, you can't just claim babies in the park.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why not? Nobody else is doing anything with them right now.

jokes.text: Oh, look, twins! No fair! I don't even have one, how come they get two?
jokes.setup: Joey and Ross are looking at old photos; Joey spots twin babies in a photo.
jokes.punchline: Joey's complaint that he doesn't even have one baby is a funny reveal of his longing — framed as competitive rather than emotional.
jokes.explanation: Light character comedy. Joey's jealousy framed as a fairness complaint is moderately funny but fairly shallow.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Are you saying that you don't want to have babies with me?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, no! I'm just saying hypothetically, if we were both still single at 40—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God! So you DO think about us not being together! What is it? Is it my hair? Do you not find me attractive anymore?

jokes.text: When we're 40, if neither of us are married, what do you say you and I have one?
jokes.setup: Joey laments he doesn't have a child; Ross offers a classic 'pact' — except about having a baby, not dating.
jokes.punchline: The proposition of a baby-making pact between two straight male friends is the implicit absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A decent joke that relies on the absurdity of a male 'backup plan' pact for having children. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Is there something un-marriable about me?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? No! Of course not. You're very marriable. I mean, if I wasn't... you know, married to you, I would totally want to marry you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Although, I gotta say, skydiving without a parachute? Now that's un-marriable.

jokes.text: Why wouldn't I be married when I'm 40? / Hypothetically, why won't I be married when I'm 40?
jokes.setup: Ross says 'hypothetically' neither of them might be married at 40; Joey takes it personally and demands to know what Ross implies.
jokes.punchline: Ross digs himself deeper with each attempt to clarify 'hypothetically,' making it worse. The question hangs uncomfortably.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe escalation as Ross's repeated 'hypothetically' makes things progressively worse. Classic sitcom awkward hole-digging.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What did you say?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I said... 'I love you too'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No you didn't!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I said it in my head!

jokes.text: Dear God, this parachute is a knapsack!
jokes.setup: Joey is pressing Ross hard about whether there's something fundamentally 'un-marriable' about him; Ross is backed into a corner and has no good answer.
jokes.punchline: Ross invents a fake emergency ('Dear God, this parachute is a knapsack!') to escape the conversation and literally runs away.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely brilliant escape joke. The specificity of 'this parachute is a knapsack' is what makes it exceptional — it's not a generic excuse, it's a hyper-specific, completely impossible scenario that is funny precisely because of how desperate and absurd it is. High quotability, excellent economy, and original. One of the most memorable jokes in the episode. Ross's cowardly retreat makes it even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Did you or did you not say 'I love you'?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I didn't say it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You totally said it!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Nuh-uh.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yuh-huh!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Nuh-uh!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yuh-huh!

jokes.text: I'm getting married today!
jokes.setup: Ross has just fled the conversation by pretending to have a parachute emergency.
jokes.punchline: He shouts 'I'm getting married today!' as an additional invented excuse while running, compounding the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A coda to the parachute gag. Gets an additional laugh riding on the momentum of the previous joke, but isn't as sharp on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So, hypothetically, if two people were living in the same apartment, and they really liked each other, that would be... okay, right? I mean, not that I'm suggesting anything. I'm just saying, in theory, if someone wanted to ask someone else if they wanted to, you know, cohabitate in a non-roommate way, how would that person go about doing that without completely freaking out the other person?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, are you asking me to move in with you?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I was asking in a very roundabout, complicated way that made it seem like I didn't know what I was talking about. If you'd just let me continue, I could have confused you for another twenty minutes or so.

jokes.text: Do you think he knew I was here?
jokes.setup: Ross has just dramatically fled the conversation with two invented excuses.
jokes.punchline: Joey genuinely wonders if Ross even noticed he was there — missing the entire point that Ross was fleeing HIM specifically.
jokes.explanation: Joey's obliviousness is the joke — he doesn't realize Ross was fleeing because of HIM. Perfect character comedy and a great button on the sequence. Joey's self-centered cluelessness is well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I want to propose to Chandler, but what if he thinks it's weird that I'm asking him? What if he wants to be the one to propose?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean, it's 2003, but apparently some traditions die hard.

jokes.text: Nice try. / Wait, wait, wait, wait.
jokes.setup: In a flashback, Chandler attempts a move on Monica or tries to leave/change the subject
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'nice try' and Chandler's desperate 'wait, wait, wait' captures the push-pull of their early relationship dynamic
jokes.explanation: Transitional beat more than a standalone joke. Mildly amusing in context but doesn't land independently.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I don't get it. What's wrong with that?

jokes.text: You are so great! I love you. / What? / Nothing! I said, you're so great, and then I just stopped talking.
jokes.setup: During a flashback, Chandler spontaneously blurts 'I love you' to Monica while they're apparently in a moment of connection.
jokes.punchline: Chandler panics and tries to claim he never said 'I love you,' offering the increasingly implausible denial 'I said you're so great and then I just stopped talking.'
jokes.explanation: Chandler's flustered cover story is a great character moment — his inability to handle emotional vulnerability expressed as panicked backpedaling. 'I said you're so great and then I just stopped talking' is a funny, specific lie. High character integration and emotional resonance makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How's Monica doing with her vows?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, she's doing great. Joey's been helping her out.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's nice.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, she's got some really beautiful stuff written down, but apparently Joey's been giving her some suggestions too. She asked me what I thought and I told her, 'Monica, that's beautiful, but maybe lose the part where you talk about how you're gonna bang Chandler like a screen door in a hurricane.'

jokes.text: You said you love me! I can't believe this. / No, I didn't. / Yes, you did. / No, I didn't! / You love me! / No, I don't! Stop it! Stop it!
jokes.setup: Chandler has just accidentally said 'I love you' and tried to take it back.
jokes.punchline: The rapid-fire 'you love me / no I don't' back-and-forth escalates to Chandler screaming 'Stop it!' at Monica for accurately repeating what he said.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the argument is funny, particularly Chandler yelling 'Stop it!' when Monica is simply repeating the truth. Good cringe energy and character work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So Monica and Chandler are getting married! That's so exciting!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, right? I'm really happy for them.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah... So when are you getting married again?

jokes.text: You know, I was thinking, what if I unpack here? / Then all your stuff would be here. / What if all my stuff was here? / Then you'd be going back and forth all the time. Doesn't make any sense. / What if we live together, and you understand what I'm saying?
jokes.setup: In another flashback, Chandler tries to propose moving in together without saying it directly.
jokes.punchline: He circles around with increasingly awkward logic until finally blurting 'What if we live together, and you understand what I'm saying?' — a hilariously inarticulate proposal.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chandler comedy. His inability to say simple emotional things directly leads to this wonderfully convoluted logic chain. 'What if we live together, and you understand what I'm saying?' is an inspired final line — he's essentially asking her to do the emotional heavy lifting for him. High character integration, good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Someone kept asking about chicken.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Chicken? Joe! JOE!

jokes.text: There's a reason why girls don't do this! / Okay, okay, okay! I'll do it.
jokes.setup: Monica is apparently trying to propose to Chandler (reversing roles), presumably getting down on one knee, but is struggling with the emotion.
jokes.punchline: Monica breaks down and admits 'there's a reason why girls don't do this' — a funny acknowledgment of gendered proposal norms — and Chandler immediately rescues her by volunteering to propose instead.
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny — Monica's confidence collapsing in the most vulnerable moment is a good character beat. The joke earns its laugh through reversal of expectations (competent Monica can't hold it together for the proposal).

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'll just tell Rachel I'm doing laundry.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Doing laundry? That's what you're calling it?

jokes.text: How is 'Monica, I love your sweet ass' inappropriate?
jokes.setup: Chandler kicked Joey and Ross out of his apartment because Joey was making inappropriate vow suggestions.
jokes.punchline: Joey genuinely doesn't understand why 'I love your sweet ass' is an inappropriate wedding vow.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey — his sincere confusion about social norms is perfectly deployed here. The specific vow ('Monica, I love your sweet ass') is funny in its earnestness. Good economy and high character integration. The delivery of the question makes it land well.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mr. Big? That's not a nickname, that's a sex thing!

jokes.text: Let's say it's lucky she's got a sweet ass because she's not so good at the writing.
jokes.setup: Joey's sweet-ass comment transitions; they're told Monica is struggling to write her vows.
jokes.punchline: Ross's response suggests Monica's good looks are compensating for her vow-writing deficiency — an accidentally harsh thing to say about his sister.
jokes.explanation: A callback to the 'sweet ass' line that also reveals Monica is struggling. Moderately funny — the dark edge of a brother essentially calling his sister dumb is a bit uncomfortable, but the joke gets by on the connection to Joey's earlier line.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I knew it! I knew it!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, what are you—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You and Chandler! Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, so you know.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: How long has this been going on?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A few months, we were going to tell everyone—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, everyone knows! Rachel knows, Joey knows, Ross knows, even Ben knows!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ben's seven!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, and he figured it out before you two told anyone.

jokes.text: Nine out of 10 marriages end in divorce. / Phoebe, that's not true. / Yeah, you're right. How's the missus?
jokes.setup: Phoebe makes a wildly inaccurate statistic about divorce to be casually negative about Chandler and Monica's upcoming marriage.
jokes.punchline: When corrected, Phoebe immediately pivots to asking 'How's the missus?' — implying she's referencing someone else's failed marriage with no segue, as if the correction didn't matter.
jokes.explanation: Deceptively sharp joke. The fake statistic is funny, but the real laugh comes from Phoebe's instant pivot — 'Yeah, you're right. How's the missus?' — implying she immediately thought of an example of a bad marriage (probably Ross). The non-sequitur pivot is very Phoebe and very economically executed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, you want to tell them we know? Okay, fine. But then I get to tell Monica that I saw her trying on wedding dresses, and I get to tell Chandler that he cried during 'The Notebook,' and I get to tell both of them that sometimes at night I can hear them through the wall, and it sounds like—

jokes.text: I can't believe they've been together 3 years. / That long? / Maybe it seems like less because they hid it from us for so long.
jokes.setup: The group reflects on how long Chandler and Monica have been together.
jokes.punchline: The acknowledgment that it seems shorter because they hid it — which is an ironic, self-aware comment about the show's secret relationship arc.
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing meta-observation about the secret relationship period. Functional but not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys know? And you're messing with us?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's... that's role reversal! I'm being Chandler!

jokes.text: Are you okay? I'm sorry. He wouldn't leave. He kept asking if I wanted chicken. / Chicken? I could eat some chicken. Hey, Joe!
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are trying to have a secret romantic moment during their hidden relationship; they're interrupted by Joey asking about chicken.
jokes.punchline: Chandler hears the word 'chicken' and immediately reveals he wants some — betraying the romantic moment for food.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom food-over-romance joke. Joey asking about chicken mid-secret-relationship is funny; Chandler's ears perking up for chicken is a fun detail. Not the sharpest but gets the job done.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, so Monica and Chandler are together, and Ross doesn't know that Rachel knows that Joey knows that Monica told Phoebe that Chandler... wait, no. Rachel told Joey that Monica told Chandler that Ross knows that... um... okay, I have no idea what's going on anymore.

jokes.text: Can I get a three-piece, some coleslaw and some beans and a Coke? / Diet Coke.
jokes.setup: Chandler calls out to Joey to order food, interrupting the romantic secret moment.
jokes.punchline: Monica corrects 'Diet Coke' — she's already managing his diet even during their secret relationship, fully in Monica mode.
jokes.explanation: Economical gem. The single word 'Diet Coke' tells you everything about Monica and Chandler's relationship dynamic — she's already controlling his diet at this early stage. Maximum character integration in minimum words. The abruptness of the correction is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't say anything about this.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Besides, I have no idea what's going on anyway.

jokes.text: You cannot tell. No one knows. / How? When? / It happened in London.
jokes.setup: Phoebe discovers Monica and Chandler's secret relationship in a flashback.
jokes.punchline: Monica's explanation that 'it happened in London' — a callback to a major show event — is played as a funny reveal.
jokes.explanation: Functional expository comedy as the flashback structure reminds audiences of key show history. Not particularly clever but serves its purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hey Chandler, I'm gonna seduce you now. So you should probably get ready for that.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm gonna start by batting my eyelashes. This is me batting my eyelashes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can see that.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Now I'm gonna touch your arm. Okay, I'm touching your arm. How's that?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's... it's good.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Now I'm gonna lean in and whisper something sexy in your ear. The thing I'm about to whisper is... 'I want you.' Okay, here I go.

jokes.text: I can't wait to be with you. I'll tell Rachel I'm doing laundry for a few hours. / Laundry? Is that my new nickname?
jokes.setup: During their secret relationship, Chandler tells Monica he'll use 'doing laundry' as a cover story for visiting her.
jokes.punchline: Monica cheekily asks if 'laundry' is her new nickname — implying she's fully aware of being treated like a chore.
jokes.explanation: Monica's mock-offended 'is that my new nickname?' is a good, quick-witted comeback. Economical and shows Monica's playful side. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm very bendy.

jokes.text: You know what your nickname is, Mr. Big...
jokes.setup: Monica asks if 'laundry' is her nickname; she then begins to offer Chandler his nickname.
jokes.punchline: She starts to say 'Mr. Big...' and is interrupted before finishing — implying a sexual nickname. The audience fills in the blank.
jokes.explanation: The interrupted compliment that implies Chandler's impressive sexual attributes. The interruption by spotting Monica and Chandler in the window is good timing. Moderate laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I can't do this anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You win. I'm not strong enough.

jokes.text: Chandler and Monica! Chandler and Monica! / Oh, my God! / Oh, my eyes! My eyes! / Phoebe! Phoebe! / It's okay! It's okay! / No! They're doing it!
jokes.setup: In a flashback, Rachel and Phoebe discover Chandler and Monica together (apparently in a compromising position through a window).
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's hysterical 'Oh, my eyes! My eyes!' reaction to seeing them is the main comedic payoff — a classic overreaction to witnessing something you can't unsee.
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, my eyes! My eyes!' is one of the most quotable lines from Friends and delivers huge impact in context. Phoebe's visceral horror at witnessing her friends' intimacy is a perfectly pitched reaction. High impact and quotability though the craft is not as sophisticated — it's really all in Phoebe's delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I love you. I love you. I love you!

jokes.text: I know! I know! / And Joey knows, but Ross doesn't know, so you have to stop screaming!
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe have just discovered Monica and Chandler together; Monica is trying to manage the discovery.
jokes.punchline: The 'who knows what' meta-tracking is funny — Monica instantly goes into information-management mode, parceling out who knows what.
jokes.explanation: Functional comedy as the secret management begins. Monica's immediate shift to damage control mode is on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Monica and Chandler? But they're so... Monica and Chandler. Wait, have they... you know?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, they slept together.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's not love, that's just sex.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, Pheebs, they're in love.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Well, why didn't you say so?

jokes.text: Oh, God! We're just so excited that you might get this apartment! / Actually, it looks really good.
jokes.setup: Ross walks in and asks what's going on after Rachel and Phoebe were screaming about Monica and Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Rachel and Phoebe instantly come up with a fake reason for their excitement — covering their discovery with false enthusiasm about an apartment.
jokes.explanation: Standard sitcom cover-story comedy. Functional but unremarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! What is going on here?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, we can explain...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Chandler?! My best friend? My sister?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We were just—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't want to hear it! Monica, you're my little sister. And Chandler, you're like a brother to me. This is... this is weird!

jokes.text: So they know you know, and they don't know that Rachel knows? / Yes, but you know what? It doesn't matter who knows what... / Or we could not tell them we know and have a little fun of our own.
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe discuss the layered secret — who knows what, and what to do with that knowledge.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's suggestion to 'not tell them we know and have a little fun' pivots the whole dynamic into active scheming.
jokes.explanation: The 'who knows who knows' sequence is classic sitcom confusion comedy. The real laugh is Phoebe pivoting from confusion to scheming — a good character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. You're moving near a Volvo dealership? Why would you move near a Volvo dealership?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We're not moving TO the dealership, Joey. We're moving to a house that happens to be near one.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh. Oh! I thought you guys were like, moving into the showroom or something.

jokes.text: Bye, Chandler. I miss you already.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Rachel have decided to mess with Monica and Chandler now that they know the secret.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe delivers an overly intimate goodbye to Chandler — 'I miss you already' — implying false romantic interest as part of the scheme to rattle him.
jokes.explanation: Good economy — Phoebe's overly intimate 'I miss you already' establishes the scheming dynamic efficiently. Chandler's clear panic implied by context.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: In my defense, I was going through a very experimental phase.

jokes.text: Did you see that? With the inappropriate and the pinching? / So now do you believe that she's attracted to me?
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just acted flirtatiously toward Chandler; Monica watches.
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks Monica if she now believes Phoebe is genuinely attracted to him — missing that it's a scheme and misreading the situation as genuine attraction.
jokes.explanation: Decent dramatic irony — the audience knows Chandler is being played while he thinks he's getting a compliment. Chandler's vanity/obliviousness is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why do I keep ending up naked in these photos?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because you have no sense of self-awareness?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not helpful, Chandler.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Oh, my God, she knows about us! Phoebe knows about us! / Well, I didn't tell them. / Them? Who's them?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica suddenly realize that Phoebe's behavior reveals she knows about their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Chandler panics and Monica accidentally reveals more people know — 'I didn't tell THEM' — causing Chandler to realize multiple people know.
jokes.explanation: The 'them? who's them?' escalation works well — Monica accidentally revealing more people know is a good twist. The unraveling of their secret is played with good energy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Maybe you should just skip the vows and go straight to the kiss.

jokes.text: They think they are so slick, messing with us! But, see, they don't know that we know that they know. / So... / Ah, yes! The messers become the messees!
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler figure out that Phoebe and Rachel are messing with them because they know the secret.
jokes.punchline: 'The messers become the messees!' — Chandler's invented word 'messees' is the comedic highlight.
jokes.explanation: 'The messers become the messees' is a highly quotable line. Chandler's invention of 'messees' is a funny linguistic flourish that fits his character perfectly — he's the kind of person who would coin a word in a moment of triumph. Good energy and high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, how did you write those vows? They were incredible!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, actually... I didn't write them. I kind of... borrowed them from Monica's vows.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You plagiarized your wife's vows?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: In my defense, they were really good, and I panicked!

jokes.text: Oh, my God, he wants me to come over and feel his bicep and more!
jokes.setup: Chandler has apparently sent a message as part of the counter-scheme to mess with Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's excited/alarmed reaction to the escalating flirtation — 'and more!' — shows the scheme is working and getting out of hand.
jokes.explanation: Funny escalation of the scheme. 'And more!' has good comedic punch from Phoebe's faux-shock delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! Why can't he just switch a couple words around? You know, like, 'I, Chandler, take you, Monica' instead of 'I, Monica, take you, Chandler.' Problem solved!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, nobody's gonna notice if you read 'em in a different order!

jokes.text: Joey? Do they know that we know? / No. / Joey! / They know you know. / I knew it!
jokes.setup: Monica asks Joey what he knows about who knows what; Joey initially lies, then immediately cracks.
jokes.punchline: Joey holds the lie for approximately one beat before capitulating and revealing the full truth — 'they know you know.'
jokes.explanation: Joey is constitutionally unable to hold a secret — this plays perfectly on that character trait. The speed of his capitulation is the joke. Good economy.

jokes.text: They don't know that we know they know we know.
jokes.setup: Monica is now tracking the layers of the meta-knowledge game.
jokes.punchline: The tongue-twisting 'they don't know that we know they know we know' is a comedic mouthful that highlights how ridiculously complicated this has gotten.
jokes.explanation: The 'they don't know that we know they know we know' line is one of the most quoted lines from this episode — a classic escalation of the who-knows-what gag to its comedic extreme. The tongue-twister quality makes it memorable and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Joey, you can't say anything. / Couldn't if I wanted to.
jokes.setup: Monica tells Joey he can't tell the others what they now know.
jokes.punchline: Joey's response — 'Couldn't if I wanted to' — implies he genuinely cannot track the layers of knowledge and is effectively neutralized as a secret-keeping risk.
jokes.explanation: One of the best understated one-liners in the episode. 'Couldn't if I wanted to' is devastating in its simplicity — Joey is so confused by the layers of the secret that he literally cannot repeat it. Perfect character integration, flawless economy. A gem.

jokes.text: This is getting out of hand! She wants me to put lotion on her! / She's bluffing! / She's not backing down. She went like this: [demonstrates]
jokes.setup: The bluffing scheme between Phoebe and Chandler is escalating; Phoebe has apparently made a flirtatious gesture.
jokes.punchline: Monica physically demonstrates Phoebe's seductive move — implying Monica herself has to act as coach for Chandler's counter-flirtation.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the bluffing game. Monica coaching Chandler on how to fake-seduce her friend is inherently absurd. The physical demonstration is an implied visual gag.

jokes.text: Okay, show him your bra. He's afraid of bras. Can't work them.
jokes.setup: Rachel is coaching Phoebe on how to push Chandler's limits in the bluffing game.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's inside knowledge that Chandler is 'afraid of bras, can't work them' is a funny specific character detail used as a tactical weapon.
jokes.explanation: Funny specific detail — Rachel weaponizes Chandler's bra incompetence. The specificity ('can't work them') is what makes it land. Good economy.

jokes.text: Wow! You didn't rip off any buttons. / It's not my first time.
jokes.setup: Monica takes off her bra (presumably to demonstrate or coach Chandler, possibly in preparation for the scheme).
jokes.punchline: Chandler's impressed that she didn't rip off any buttons; Monica's confident 'it's not my first time' implies practiced expertise.
jokes.explanation: Good economy — the callback to the bra-fear with Monica demonstrating calm competence. 'It's not my first time' works as an understated brag.

jokes.text: Well, come here. I'm very happy we're gonna have all the sex. / You should be. I'm very bendy.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is seducing Chandler as part of the bluffing scheme, escalating with physical promises.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's declaration 'I'm very bendy' is delivered with complete sincerity — a funny, specific, Phoebe-ish thing to say during fake seduction.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm very bendy' is exactly the kind of non-sequitur specific detail that is totally Phoebe — it's weirdly earnest, oddly specific, and completely disarming. High character integration and quotability. The sincerity of delivery makes it funnier.

jokes.text: You should be. I'm very bendy.
jokes.setup: Chandler says he's happy they're 'gonna have all the sex'; Phoebe responds in kind
jokes.punchline: 'I'm very bendy' — a matter-of-fact disclosure that is both an overshare and a perfectly timed counter-escalation
jokes.explanation: Perfect counter-punch to 'all the sex.' Three words, delivered deadpan, that work as both a Phoebe-character joke (her lack of filter and casual disclosure) and as a perfect escalation. The matter-of-fact delivery is what makes it land — she's not embarrassed, not winking, just stating a fact. Extremely quotable. High craft score justified by economy and character integration.

jokes.text: I'm gonna kiss you now. / Not if I kiss you first.
jokes.setup: The bluffing game has escalated to the point where both Phoebe and Chandler are threatening to actually kiss each other — neither willing to back down.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'not if I kiss you first' is the game reaching maximum absurdity — both are now actively competing to kiss someone they don't want to kiss.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of competitive fake-seduction to 'not if I kiss you first' is absurdist and funny. Good cringe energy as the bluff threatens to actually happen.

jokes.text: I guess there's nothing left for us to do but kiss. / Here it comes. Our first kiss.
jokes.setup: Both have been threatening to kiss; neither has backed down; they narrate the inevitability
jokes.punchline: The mutual self-narration of 'here it comes, our first kiss' treats the fake kiss like a sporting event — the deadpan commentary is funnier than any actual kiss
jokes.explanation: Good bit — the meta-commentary on their own fake romance while both are clearly terrified is very funny. The formal 'our first kiss' as an announcement is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: Okay, okay, okay, fine, you win! / Ha! / I can't have sex with you. / Why not? / Because I'm in love with Monica. / You're what? / Love her! That's right, I love her! I love her!
jokes.setup: The fake seduction game has gone so far that Chandler breaks first — but instead of a normal capitulation, he blurts out that he loves Monica.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's emphatic 'I love her! I love her!' declaration is funny because it's such an over-the-top emotional outburst born out of a game of chicken, and because Phoebe is genuinely stunned to learn it's love, not just sex.
jokes.explanation: A great comedic-emotional moment. The setup is a game of bluffing chicken; the payoff is Chandler accidentally confessing genuine love. 'I love her! I love her!' repeated with increasing desperation is very funny while also being genuinely sweet. Phoebe's 'you're WHAT?' reaction is perfect. The joke works on multiple levels.

jokes.text: Love her! That's right, I love her! I love her!
jokes.setup: Chandler has just admitted he's in love with Monica; he now shouts it with abandon
jokes.punchline: The repeated declaration — escalating from admission to full shout — works as comedy because Chandler, who struggles with emotional expression throughout the series, is suddenly completely unleashed
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is entirely in the character reversal — Chandler, who couldn't even whisper 'I love you' in a flashback earlier this episode, is now bellowing it repeatedly. The contrast with joke #20 makes this land much harder for attentive viewers.

jokes.text: I love you, Monica. / I love you too, Chandler.
jokes.setup: Chandler's declaration of love has just come spilling out in front of Phoebe; Monica hears and responds.
jokes.punchline: The sweet exchange of 'I love yous' is both genuine and comedic — it's funny because it took an absurd bluffing game to get Chandler to say it properly.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to Chandler's emotional journey through the episode's flashbacks. Earns its emotional beat through comedic context.

jokes.text: I thought you guys were doing it. I didn't know you were in love.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica just had their emotional love declaration in front of Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's revelation that she only knew about the sex, not the love — 'I didn't know you were in love' — is hilariously delivered as if love is the surprising part, not the secret relationship.
jokes.explanation: A great Phoebe line. The implication that the sex was known and unremarkable, but the LOVE is the shocking revelation, is a lovely comic inversion. Perfectly in character — Phoebe is the most spiritually open and least judgemental about sex. High character integration and excellent economy.

jokes.text: So that's it, it's over. Everybody knows. / Well, actually, Ross doesn't. / We'd appreciate if no one told him yet.
jokes.setup: The secret is finally out; Monica and Chandler think everyone knows
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'well, actually, Ross doesn't' is a callback to the ongoing Ross-is-always-last-to-know gag, and 'we'd appreciate if no one told him yet' extends the joke by making Ross's ignorance a deliberate ongoing state
jokes.explanation: Good running-gag payoff. 'We'd appreciate if no one told him yet' is a funny button — they've just had a cathartic emotional revelation but immediately want to continue excluding Ross, treating his ignorance as a preference rather than a problem.

jokes.text: No. / What are you doing? / Get off my sister!
jokes.setup: Everyone agrees not to tell Ross yet; immediately after, Ross walks in on Chandler and Monica.
jokes.punchline: Ross's visceral 'Get off my sister!' reaction — the comedic payoff is both the discovery AND the punchline 'No' (from Monica or Chandler) followed by the outraged sibling reaction.
jokes.explanation: 'Get off my sister!' is a classic Ross outrage line that works as both a funny callback (they agreed not to tell him) and a great character moment. The staging — immediately after they all agree he won't find out — is a perfect sitcom timing beat. High impact.

jokes.text: Your friends getting married, it's gotta change things. / You think it'll be that different? / How could it not be? Soon, they're gonna have kids... and hang out with other couples who have kids. / And maybe they'll leave the city... to be near a Volvo dealership.
jokes.setup: Ross and Joey reflect on Monica and Chandler's upcoming marriage and what it means for their friend group.
jokes.punchline: Joey's escalating anxiety about change lands on the hyper-specific, oddly mundane 'Volvo dealership' — a funny symbol of suburban adult life.
jokes.explanation: 'Leave the city to be near a Volvo dealership' is a great punchline — the specificity of 'Volvo' (not just 'suburbs' or 'the country') makes it funnier and captures exactly the right flavor of boring adult domesticity. Joey's sincere anxiety about losing friends to adulthood is both touching and funny.

jokes.text: And maybe they'll leave the city... to be near a Volvo dealership.
jokes.setup: Joey and Ross are discussing how marriage will change Monica and Chandler; Ross mentions they might leave the city
jokes.punchline: 'To be near a Volvo dealership' — the specific, suburban horror of the most un-hip reason to leave New York City
jokes.explanation: Very specific and well-chosen. 'Volvo dealership' as a symbol of boring suburban conformity is both funny and culturally precise — Volvo as the responsible-parent car is a sharp shorthand. The specificity elevates what could have been a generic suburban-life joke into something memorable.

jokes.text: It'll be okay, Joe. / Sorry. I just... I like things the way they are.
jokes.setup: Joey is worried about change; Ross reassures him. Joey's sincerity is itself slightly funny.
jokes.punchline: Joey's heartfelt 'I like things the way they are' is played straight — the comedy is that this fear of change is delivered by the most childlike member of the group.
jokes.explanation: More of a character/emotional beat than a pure joke. The comedy is light — Joey's sincere sweetness is endearing but not particularly funny.

jokes.text: Who's this little naked guy? / That little naked guy would be me. / Look at the little thing. / Yes. Yes, fine, that is my penis. Can we be grownups now?
jokes.setup: Joey and Ross are looking through old photographs and Joey spots a baby photo of Ross — apparently a nude one.
jokes.punchline: Ross's escalating embarrassment culminates in 'Yes, fine, that is my penis. Can we be grownups now?' — a mortified, exasperated declaration.
jokes.explanation: 'Yes, fine, that is my penis. Can we be grownups now?' is a solid, quotable line. The escalation from Joey's curiosity to Ross's exasperated formal acknowledgment of his baby penis is funny. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Looks like a fun gang.
jokes.setup: Ross and Joey are looking at an old photo of Monica's grandmother 'and the gang' at a 1930s coffee shop.
jokes.punchline: Joey's breezy 'looks like a fun gang' — appreciating what appears to be a Prohibition-era social circle as simply a fun group of people.
jokes.explanation: Light observational moment. Joey's simple appreciation of old photos is mildly charming but not a strong joke.

jokes.text: Look, look, look! I got Monica naked. / Let me see. / No, that would be me again.
jokes.setup: Joey triumphantly announces he found a nude photo of Monica in the album.
jokes.punchline: Ross looks and confirms it's another nude baby photo of himself — 'No, that would be me again.'
jokes.explanation: A great callback joke. The 'No, that would be me again' punchline is excellent — the repetition of the Ross-naked-baby-photo gag with a fresh angle (Joey's excitement over Monica deflated by it being Ross again) is well-structured. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: You can get a Volvo. If that's what you really want.
jokes.setup: Joey and Ross are talking to Monica and Chandler about the wedding; Joey had been worried about them leaving for suburbia.
jokes.punchline: Joey's attempt at being generous and accepting — 'you can get a Volvo if that's what you really want' — delivered as a reluctant concession.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Volvo dealership line. Joey's magnanimous permission for them to have a Volvo is sweet and funny — he's given in to accepting change but needs to verbalize it through his chosen symbol of adulthood.

jokes.text: [Reading vows] Oh, that's beautiful. / Funny one! That's good!
jokes.setup: Monica's and Chandler's vows are read aloud to the group (separately); we hear the group's reactions but not the vow content.
jokes.punchline: The vow reading is played entirely through audience reactions — 'that's beautiful' and 'funny one! that's good!' — implying Monica's vows swing between sincere and funny.
jokes.explanation: A clever structural choice — keeping the vow content private but letting us see the emotional range through reactions. 'Funny one! That's good!' is itself a funny, excited reaction.

jokes.text: Monica, will you marry me? / What? I don't get it. / Oh, yeah!
jokes.setup: Chandler's vow apparently ends with a proposal to Monica — but since they're already engaged, the group is momentarily confused.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'What? I don't get it' is funny because she's genuinely confused; Joey's belated 'Oh, yeah!' shows him catching up.
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the proposal-in-the-vow confuses the group before the penny drops. Joey's delayed comprehension is a reliable laugh.

jokes.text: Man, this is hilarious! / Chandler! / Don't worry, honey. We'll make yours funnier.
jokes.setup: Chandler's vows are apparently hilarious; Monica is offended because hers are more sincere.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's oblivious 'Don't worry, honey. We'll make yours funnier' — implying Monica's sincere vows are inferior for not being funny.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's clueless offer to 'make hers funnier' is a good character moment — it shows his comedy-as-defense-mechanism applied to the most inappropriate moment.

jokes.text: Dude... / I have never known love like this. / You really like it? / Dude!
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Joey and Ross what they think of his vows.
jokes.punchline: Joey's complete inability to articulate his emotion beyond 'Dude' — and the escalation of a second, more emphatic 'Dude!' — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Joey's vocabulary collapsing under emotional impact into simply 'Dude' is perfect character comedy. The escalation from 'Dude...' to a more emphatic 'Dude!' is a great two-beat structure. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: How did you write this? / I stole Monica's and changed the name. / You can't do that! / If he goes first, he can!
jokes.setup: Everyone is amazed by Chandler's beautiful vows; Ross asks how he wrote them.
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually admits he stole Monica's vows and just changed the name. Monica objects; Joey immediately finds the loophole: 'If he goes first, he can!'
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and a near-perfect sitcom tag. The setup has been building all episode — Chandler struggling to write vows, Monica writing something beautiful. The reveal that he simply stole hers and changed the name is a hysterical subversion of the entire emotional journey. Joey's immediate finding of the loophole ('If he goes first, he can!') is the second punchline that escalates the laugh. Excellent structure, brilliant character integration (only Chandler would do this, only Joey would immediately find the workaround), and maximum economy. This is the episode's comedic peak.

jokes.text: How did you write this? / I stole Monica's and changed the name.
jokes.setup: Ross is moved by Chandler's vows and asks how he wrote something so beautiful
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually admits he plagiarized Monica's vows and just changed the name — the ultimate lazy shortcut that works perfectly as the episode's final joke
jokes.explanation: The episode's best-structured joke and arguably its strongest overall. It's a perfect callback to the opening joke about buying vows — Chandler's laziness about vow-writing is the first joke of the episode, and 'I stole Monica's and changed the name' is its ultimate expression. The structure is impeccable: build an episode around a character struggling with something, have him appear to succeed magnificently, then reveal the most lazily ingenious solution imaginable. Character integration is very high — this is entirely Chandler. 'You can't do that! / If he goes first, he can!' (the button) makes it even better. This is in legitimate 8.5+ territory.

tmdb_overview: Monica and Chandler are getting married in four weeks and have to write their vows, but neither has a clue what to say, so they reflect on their past. In the end, the only real problem is who will be saying the vows first.
insight: Chandler's panic escalates relentlessly through 42 jokes—wedding-day chaos peaks at 2.66 gags per minute.
